question_data.passage:
The notion that human beings possess an innate moral sense has long divided philosophers. On one side stand those who, following Hume, argue that morality is rooted in sentiment rather than reason. According to this view, our judgments about right and wrong are not the conclusions of logical arguments but the expressions of feelings shaped by evolution and culture. When we condemn cruelty, we do so not because we have deduced its wrongness from first principles, but because the suffering of others provokes in us an instinctive revulsion. Reason, in Hume's famous phrase, is and ought only to be the slave of the passions.

Opposed to this stand the rationalists, who follow Kant in insisting that genuine moral judgments must be grounded in reason alone. To act morally, on this view, is to act in accordance with principles that any rational being could endorse. Feelings are notoriously variable and partial; they make us favor our friends over strangers, our compatriots over foreigners. Only reason can extract us from such bias and disclose obligations that bind us universally.

Recent work in moral psychology, however, suggests that the dichotomy between sentiment and reason is itself misleading. Empirical studies indicate that moral judgments typically arise rapidly and intuitively, with reasoning entering only afterwards to justify what feeling has already decided. Yet this does not vindicate Hume entirely. For the very intuitions on which we rely have been shaped, over generations, by reasoned discourse: by religious teachings, philosophical arguments, legal codes, and public deliberation. What presents itself to consciousness as raw feeling may in fact be the sediment of countless arguments long since absorbed into habit.

If this account is correct, then the question is not whether morality rests on sentiment or reason, but how the two interact across historical time. Moral progress, when it occurs, may consist precisely in reasoned challenges that gradually reshape our intuitions, until what once seemed natural and unobjectionable comes to feel monstrous, and what once seemed monstrous comes to feel ordinary.

questions.stem: What does the author ultimately suggest about the debate between sentiment and reason in moral judgment?
choices: Hume's account has been decisively confirmed by recent moral psychology.
Kant's rationalism remains the only defensible position.
The opposition between the two is misleading because reason and sentiment shape one another over time.
Empirical research has shown that moral judgments are entirely arbitrary.
questions.explanation: 最終段落で「問題は道徳が感情か理性かではなく、両者が歴史的時間の中でどう相互作用するかだ」と述べている。よって両者を対立させる枠組み自体が誤りだとする選択肢3が正解。1, 2 はいずれか一方を支持しすぎ、4 は本文と無関係。

question_data.passage:
It is often said that the great achievement of modern science was to banish purpose from nature. Where Aristotle had seen acorns striving toward oak-hood and stones falling because they sought their natural place, Galileo and Newton described a universe of inert matter governed by mathematical law. The world, on this picture, does not aim at anything; it merely behaves. Every appearance of purposeful arrangement, from the eye to the ecosystem, must be explained as the by-product of blind mechanism.

Yet purpose has proved remarkably difficult to eliminate. Biologists, who are perhaps the most committed naturalists, find themselves unable to describe their subject without speaking of what hearts are for, what wings are designed to do, what genes are supposed to accomplish. Such talk is dismissed as mere shorthand, a convenient substitute for the cumbersome language of natural selection. Yet the shorthand persists because it captures something real: organisms are not random aggregates of matter but functional wholes whose parts can be understood only in relation to the activities they enable.

Some philosophers have argued that this stubborn presence of teleological language reveals a limit of the mechanical worldview. To understand why a heart pumps blood, it is not enough to specify the physical forces involved; one must also grasp the role pumping plays in the maintenance of the organism. Such explanations are not reducible to laws of motion, however much we might wish them to be. Functional understanding, on this view, constitutes an autonomous mode of knowledge, neither superstitious vestige nor disposable metaphor.

The debate matters beyond biology. If teleological notions are indispensable in explaining living systems, the same may hold for human action, history, and culture. The intellectual ambition that began with the rejection of purpose may, paradoxically, be forced to accommodate it once again, this time on terms that science cannot dismiss as merely pre-modern.

questions.stem: Which of the following best captures the author's central claim?
choices: Modern science has fully succeeded in eliminating purpose from our understanding of nature.
Teleological language in biology is merely a convenient shorthand with no real explanatory value.
The persistence of functional explanation suggests that purpose cannot be wholly banished from scientific thought.
Aristotelian physics should replace modern mechanical accounts of the natural world.
questions.explanation: 第3段落で目的論的説明は単なる略記ではなく自律的な知の様式だと述べ、最終段落でその含意は生物学を超えると展開している。よって3が正解。1は本文の主張と逆、2は著者が否定する見方、4は極端すぎる。

question_data.passage:
The history of cartography offers a curious lesson about the relationship between knowledge and representation. For most of human history, maps were not primarily instruments of navigation. Medieval European maps placed Jerusalem at the center of the world, surrounded by the three known continents arranged according to theological symbolism rather than geographical accuracy. To consult such a map was not to find one's way through space but to locate oneself within a sacred order.

The gradual transformation of the map into a tool of accurate spatial representation was inseparable from the rise of commercial empires and centralized states. Merchants needed reliable charts to send ships to distant ports; governments needed surveys to tax landholders and conscript soldiers. The map became, in effect, an instrument of administration, and its claim to objectivity reflected the interests of those who commissioned it. The blank spaces on colonial maps, for instance, were rarely empty; they were inhabited by peoples whose presence the cartographer chose, or was instructed, not to record.

This is not to dismiss modern cartography as mere ideology. The advances in surveying, projection, and triangulation that produced the precise maps of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries represent genuine cognitive achievements. Yet the very precision of such maps can mislead us. By presenting the world as a uniform grid of measurable distances, they encourage us to forget that any map is also a selection: it shows what its makers considered worth showing, and silently excludes what they did not.

What we call objectivity in representation is rarely the absence of perspective. More often, it is a perspective so successful, so widely shared, that it ceases to be visible as a perspective at all. The medieval map advertised its values openly; the modern map conceals them beneath the appearance of neutral fact. To read either intelligently is to ask not only what the map shows, but what its silences signify.

questions.stem: What is the author's main argument about modern maps?
choices: They are technically inferior to medieval maps because they lack symbolic depth.
Their apparent objectivity disguises the selective interests of their makers.
They have rendered all earlier forms of cartography obsolete and worthless.
They prove that human knowledge is fundamentally subjective and unreliable.
questions.explanation: 最終段落で「客観性とは視点の不在ではなく、可視化されないほど共有された視点である」と述べ、近代地図はその選択性を中立的事実の外観の下に隠していると指摘している。よって2が正解。1は誤り、3は本文より強すぎ、4は懐疑論への飛躍。

question_data.passage:
Among the more curious features of human cognition is our reluctance to believe what we know. Smokers continue to smoke, fully informed of the statistical link between tobacco and disease. Citizens of low-lying coastal cities continue to plan their futures as though sea levels were stable, despite the unanimous testimony of the scientific community. The information is available; the implications are clear; yet the corresponding action does not follow. Why?

One traditional answer appeals to weakness of will. We know what we ought to do but lack the discipline to do it. This explanation, while occasionally apt, treats knowledge as a single uniform thing, and fails to capture the layered structure of human belief. A second account points to motivated reasoning: we discount evidence that threatens our interests or identity, and amplify whatever supports them. This too has explanatory force, but it leaves something unsaid.

A more illuminating perspective, perhaps, is that knowing a fact and inhabiting it are different cognitive operations. To know that the climate is changing is to be able to assert the proposition, to recall it on examination, to accept its inferential consequences when presented in argument. To inhabit the same fact is to feel its weight in one's daily decisions, to reorganize one's plans around it, to perceive the world differently because of it. Most of what we know remains, in this sense, uninhabited.

If this distinction is correct, then the political problem of communicating scientific consensus is not chiefly one of distributing information. The information has been distributed. What has not been achieved is the more difficult task of helping people inhabit what they already know. This requires not louder repetition of the facts but the cultivation of imagination, narrative, and shared practice, by which abstract propositions are translated into experienced reality. Without such cultivation, knowledge will continue to coexist, comfortably, with its own denial.

questions.stem: What does the author identify as the most important obstacle to acting on scientific knowledge such as climate change?
choices: A simple lack of access to reliable scientific information.
A failure to translate abstract knowledge into lived experience and practice.
An innate human incapacity to understand statistical evidence.
The deliberate suppression of scientific findings by political authorities.
questions.explanation: 著者は「知ること」と「住まうこと」を区別し、第3・4段落で抽象命題を経験された現実に翻訳する想像力・物語・実践の涵養が欠けていると主張する。よって2が正解。1は本文で「情報は配布済」と否定、3, 4は本文で扱われていない。

question_data.passage: What we call common sense is in many respects the deposit of forgotten controversies. (X) The propositions that strike us today as too obvious to require argument were, in earlier centuries, the contested conclusions of fierce intellectual struggles, accepted only after the alternatives had been weighed and gradually abandoned. The very obviousness of such truths is therefore not evidence of their self-evident character; it is evidence of how thoroughly the arguments that established them have been forgotten. To recover those arguments is to recognize that what we now take for granted was once the hard-won achievement of disputation, and might, under different historical pressures, have been otherwise.

question_data.passage: The relationship between language and thought has long fascinated philosophers and linguists alike. (X) So thoroughly does the structure of our native tongue shape the contours of our reflection that, in attempting to think outside its categories, we resemble swimmers struggling against a current we cannot see. This does not mean, however, that translation between languages is impossible, only that it is more demanding than ordinary speakers commonly suppose. To render a sentence faithfully from one language into another is not to substitute equivalent words but to reconstruct, in the target tongue, a pattern of emphasis and implication that the original made available to its speakers as a matter of course.

question_data.passage:
Informed consent has become one of the central pillars of modern medical ethics, yet its practical implementation remains far more complex than the principle itself. The doctrine, which emerged in its modern form during the second half of the twentieth century, holds that competent adults have the right to decide what is done to their bodies, and that physicians are obliged to disclose the relevant facts about proposed treatments before proceeding. Patients, on this view, are not passive recipients of medical authority but active partners in clinical decisions.

In practice, however, several difficulties arise. The first concerns the quantity and complexity of medical information. A complete account of the risks and benefits of a single intervention may run to dozens of pages of statistical data, much of it derived from studies whose methodology lay specialists themselves struggle to evaluate. Patients facing a diagnosis are rarely in the cognitive or emotional state to absorb such material, and physicians, working under severe time pressure, often resort to brief verbal summaries that inevitably simplify the underlying evidence.

A second difficulty involves the asymmetry of expertise. The physician's recommendation, however carefully framed as one option among others, carries an authority that few patients feel free to question. Studies have repeatedly shown that the way information is presented, the order in which alternatives are listed, and the verbal cues that accompany the discussion exert a substantial influence on patient choice. What appears to be autonomous decision-making is often, on closer examination, the gentle channeling of choice along a path the physician has implicitly recommended.

These considerations do not invalidate the principle of informed consent; they complicate its application. Genuine respect for patient autonomy may require not merely the formal disclosure of facts but the cultivation of an environment in which patients feel genuinely empowered to question, to seek second opinions, and to refuse interventions that their physicians consider advisable. Without such an environment, informed consent risks becoming a procedural ritual rather than the substantive moral protection it was designed to be.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is the author's principal concern about the current practice of informed consent?
choices: Patients should be denied access to detailed medical information because it tends to confuse them.
Physicians no longer recognize informed consent as an important ethical obligation.
Although the principle is sound, in practice it can become a formal ritual that fails to protect genuine autonomy.
The doctrine should be abandoned because patients lack the expertise to make medical decisions.
questions.explanation: 最終段落で「これらの考察は原則を無効にするのではなく、その適用を複雑にする」「真の自律尊重には形式的開示以上のものが必要」「さもなければ手続き上の儀礼になる危険」と述べている。3 が正解。1, 4 は本文と反対、2 は本文に根拠なし。

question_data.passage:
Vaccine hesitancy has emerged in recent decades as a significant public health challenge, even in societies where vaccination programs have historically achieved high coverage. Public health authorities have often responded by intensifying communication campaigns that emphasize the safety and efficacy of vaccines, on the assumption that hesitancy stems primarily from a deficit of accurate information. This approach, while well-intentioned, has yielded disappointing results, and in some cases has appeared to deepen the very mistrust it was designed to dispel.

Research in social psychology suggests that the deficit model misconstrues the nature of the problem. Hesitant parents, when interviewed, generally do not lack access to scientific information; many have read extensively, albeit selectively, about the topic. What characterizes their position is not ignorance but a particular relationship to authority. They are reluctant to accept the testimony of institutions, including pharmaceutical companies, government agencies, and mainstream medical bodies, whose motives they regard with suspicion. Confronted with additional pronouncements from these same institutions, they perceive not reassurance but reinforcement of the imbalance of power they already resent.

More productive interventions have tended to operate at the level of trust rather than information. When health workers from within the affected community engage hesitant families in extended conversation, listen seriously to their concerns, and acknowledge legitimate historical reasons for skepticism, attitudes can shift. Such work is slow, labor-intensive, and rarely produces the kind of statistical results that public health agencies use to demonstrate progress. Yet it appears to address the actual mechanism of hesitancy in a way that mass communication campaigns do not.

The lesson extends beyond vaccination. Across a range of public health domains, the assumption that scientifically endorsed behavior will follow once the relevant facts are widely known has proved repeatedly inadequate. The challenge is not merely epistemic but social: to rebuild, in communities where it has eroded, the kind of trust without which evidence-based recommendations cannot reliably translate into action.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the author's view on addressing vaccine hesitancy?
choices: The most effective response is to repeat scientific information more loudly and frequently.
Hesitancy is primarily caused by a lack of education that can be remedied through standard schooling.
Effective responses must address eroded trust through community-based engagement, not merely the supply of information.
Hesitant parents should be legally compelled to vaccinate their children regardless of their concerns.
questions.explanation: 第3・4段落で著者は情報伝達ではなく信頼の再構築が鍵であり、コミュニティ内の対話と歴史的経緯の認識が必要だと論じている。3 が正解。1 は deficit model 批判と矛盾、2 は本文の趣旨を取り違え、4 は本文に根拠なし。

question_data.passage:
The treatment of mental illness has undergone a profound transformation over the past half-century, and yet stigma surrounding psychiatric conditions remains stubbornly resistant to change. Pharmacological advances and the gradual integration of mental health services into general medical practice have made effective treatments more widely available than at any previous point in history. Public awareness campaigns, supported by celebrities and politicians who disclose their own struggles, have sought to normalize the experience of mental illness and to encourage those affected to seek help.

Despite these efforts, surveys consistently reveal that individuals with diagnosed mental disorders continue to face discrimination in employment, housing, and personal relationships. Many delay seeking care for months or years out of concern about how a diagnosis might affect their professional standing. Even within healthcare itself, there is evidence that physical complaints presented by patients with psychiatric histories are sometimes dismissed or attributed too readily to their underlying mental conditions, a phenomenon that has been termed diagnostic overshadowing.

The persistence of stigma reflects, in part, the special character of psychiatric disease. Unlike most physical illnesses, mental disorders manifest themselves through alterations of behavior, mood, and judgment, the very capacities by which we ordinarily evaluate other people. To label someone as mentally ill is therefore to call into question their reliability as a social agent in ways that diagnoses of cancer or diabetes do not. The boundary between illness and personality remains, in popular perception, uncomfortably blurred.

Reducing stigma will likely require more than improved public messaging. It will require institutional reforms that remove penalties for seeking treatment, training that helps clinicians recognize and counter their own biases, and a sustained cultural conversation that distinguishes the symptoms of illness from the identity of the person who experiences them. Without such structural change, the gap between what we know about mental health and how we actually treat those affected by it is likely to remain wide.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why has stigma toward mental illness been particularly difficult to overcome?
choices: Because pharmacological treatments for mental illness are still completely ineffective.
Because psychiatric conditions affect the very behaviors and judgments through which we assess one another.
Because public awareness campaigns have deliberately concealed the realities of mental illness.
Because most physicians refuse to recognize mental illness as a legitimate medical category.

question_data.passage: End-of-life care raises ethical questions that admit of no easy resolution. (X) Among the most difficult is whether the obligation of physicians to preserve life should yield, in certain circumstances, to the equally weighty obligation to relieve suffering when no further benefit can be expected from continued treatment. Different jurisdictions have answered this question differently, and the medical profession itself remains divided. What is generally agreed, however, is that the patient's own wishes, when they have been clearly expressed in advance, deserve substantial weight, even if those wishes diverge from what family members or attending physicians would themselves have chosen.

question_data.passage: Epidemiological research has long depended on the careful interpretation of statistical associations. (X) Not until investigators have systematically excluded the possibility that an apparent link between exposure and disease arises from chance, bias, or some unmeasured factor common to both, can they reasonably entertain the hypothesis of a causal relationship. The history of public health is replete with examples of associations that initially seemed compelling but which dissolved on closer examination, as well as causes that escaped notice for years because the relevant data had not yet been collected. Methodological rigor is therefore not a luxury but a precondition of the discipline.

question_data.passage:
The recent revival of industrial policy in advanced economies marks a striking reversal of the orthodoxy that prevailed for several decades. From the 1980s onward, governments in Europe, North America, and Japan increasingly embraced the view that the state should refrain from picking winners among industries. Markets, it was argued, allocate resources more efficiently than bureaucrats, and attempts to direct investment toward favored sectors had produced expensive failures more often than transformative successes. Privatization, deregulation, and trade liberalization formed the practical expression of this consensus.

In the past decade, however, the consensus has begun to fracture. The shock of the financial crisis raised doubts about the self-regulating capacity of markets, and the rise of China demonstrated that a state-directed approach to industrial development could, under certain conditions, produce remarkable results. More recently, concerns about supply chain resilience and the strategic importance of advanced semiconductors have led even market-oriented governments to commit substantial public resources to favored industries, often justified in the language of national security rather than industrial policy.

The new interventionism, however, faces challenges that the older industrial policies did not. Global supply chains are now far more deeply integrated than in earlier decades, and an attempt by one country to onshore strategic production frequently provokes retaliation or imitation by others, with the cumulative effect of fragmenting the very markets on which efficient production depends. The fiscal cost of such policies, moreover, is rarely matched by clear criteria for evaluating success. Subsidies disbursed today may sustain politically favored firms long after their original strategic rationale has lapsed.

Whether the new industrial policy will prove more successful than its predecessors will depend less on the rhetoric of national renewal than on the quality of institutions that design and implement it. Without rigorous mechanisms for choosing targets, monitoring performance, and withdrawing support when objectives are unmet, the danger is that strategic ambition will collapse, in time, into ordinary political favoritism, with all the inefficiencies the previous era had hoped to eliminate.

questions.stem: What is the author's principal warning regarding the recent revival of industrial policy?
choices: It will inevitably succeed because state-led approaches have already proved superior to market mechanisms.
Without strong institutions to evaluate and discipline interventions, it risks degenerating into political favoritism.
It should be abandoned immediately in favor of a return to the deregulatory consensus of the 1980s.
Its primary purpose should be to reproduce China's economic model in advanced Western economies.
questions.explanation: 最終段落で著者は「修辞より制度の質が決定的」「目標選定・成果監視・支援撤退の厳格な仕組みがなければ戦略的野心は通常の政治的優遇に堕する」と警告している。2 が正解。1, 3, 4 はいずれも本文の慎重な立場と異なる極端な選択肢。
